title: Could This New Legislation Protect Historic Sites From Trump's Wrath?
description:
News
                As a heavily Trump-appointed council
body:
News
                As a heavily Trump-appointed council tries to loosen preservation safeguards, Democrats are spearheading the PRESERVE Act to protect publicly commissioned art.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
             Detail of Ben Shahn mural at the Wilbur J. Cohen Federal Building in Washington, DC (photo Carol M. Highsmith via Library of Congress)
    
        
            As President Donald Trump and his appointees escalate their legislative attacks against historic sites and the artworks housed within them, Democrats and preservationist groups are pushing for protective countermeasures.On July 24, the heavily Trump-appointed Advisory Council on Historic Preservation (ACHP) advanced a proposal that could diminish legal protections of historic sites. The 16–5 vote approved revisions to Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act, a measure that mandates federal agencies to consider possible damages to historically significant sites before undertaking construction projects.

title: 2,300-Year-Old Fragment of Homer’s “Odyssey” Now on View at The Met
description:
News
                The papyrus fragment contains three lines from Book 20 of the epic that don’t appear in the modern text.
body:
News
                The papyrus fragment contains three lines from Book 20 of the epic that don’t appear in the modern text.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            A papyrus fragment of Homer's Odyssey on view at The Metropolitan Museum of Art (photo Rebecca Schear, all courtesy The Met)
    
        
            The subway trek to the Upper East Side is slightly easier than Odysseus's journey across the Mediterranean, provided the 6 train is running. For those who prevail, their reward will be plentiful: A 2,300-year-old papyrus fragment containing parts of Homer's Odyssey is now on view at the Metropolitan Museum of Art. The institution announced this week that the object would emerge from its long retirement on August 5. The fragment is now on public view at the museum in Gallery 162.In a video accompanying The Met's announcement, Séan Hemingway, curator in charge of Greek and Roman art, described the papyrus as “the earliest preserved fragment of Homer's Odyssey that we have today.”

title: Savneet Talwar, Anna Boghiguian, Iris van Herpen
description:
Weekly Newsletter
                A never-before-published interview with Simone Forti, pleating at the Brooklyn Museum with an
body:
Weekly Newsletter
                A never-before-published interview with Simone Forti, pleating at the Brooklyn Museum with an elite designer, and heartbreaking drawings by children held at ICE facilities. 
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            Sunset over Brooklyn at the end of a workday puts my mind at relative ease. A discarded still life of white roses in a golden frame resting against a pile of black trash bags outside someone's house ends up being the most memorable art installation of the week. A new storefront church opens near my house; I see it one night when I go to buy milk for the kids. It's got a lobby with fancy-looking brown leather sofas for the faithful to sit comfortably on. I pass by a bookstore and see a photobook by Hans Wilschut titled Beirut, Epi-Centre Ville. It traces the impact of the devastating blast of 2020 on the city's streets and soul. The book piques my interest, but I keep walking and see a Honda Civic with a license plate that reads "FATIGUE." I pull my phone out to snap a picture of it, and get reminded that it's August 4, the sixth anniversary of the blast. At work, we publish a piece about desperate drawings made by immigrant children held in ICE detention camps. It breaks my heart to pieces. News about community members fighting to reinstate SAIC professor Savneet Talwar, who was unjustly put on leave for asking students to imagine treatment for a pro-Palestinian protester, put my heart back together again.Outside an open studios event in Brooklyn, I talk with an artist who makes the case for "holding on to hope.""Isn't hope for people who have no power?" I ask her. "Exactly," she says. —Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief

	
		
			AI Companies Are Pulping Our Humanity
		
	
	
		After Spanish physician and theologian Michael Servetus was burnt at the stake in 1553 for religious heresy, only three surviving copies of his The Restoration of Christianity would be spared from the bonfire. One particular copy, now held by the University of Edinburgh library, is ironically believed to have been personally saved by the Protestant leader John Calvin, who was responsible for Servetus’s execution in Geneva. Anyone familiar with Calvin, who bragged in a letter that he had “purged the Church of so pernicious a monster,” knows that the book wasn’t preserved due to affection for Servetus, but rather a bibliophile’s sentiment — even a doctrinaire, zealous, tyrannical bibliophile. 
      
      And yet, as bizarre as Calvin’s motivations might have been, he’s still not as noxious as the artificial intelligence companies, including Anthropic, that have been involved in bulk purchasing, digitizing, and then pulping out-of-print books to train their large language models. Calvin at least had the excuse of his God; AI companies don’t even have that. | Ed Simon

title: All-Night Art Heist in Italy Suspected to Be ‘Some Sort of Revenge’
description: On July 28, a group of 10 people ransacked the headquarters of the Italian fuel distribution company, Lilli Petroli, in L’Aquila, located in Italy’s
body:
On July 28, a group of 10 people ransacked the headquarters of the Italian fuel distribution company, Lilli Petroli, in L’Aquila, located in Italy’s Abruzzo region, spending as long as eight hours on the premises before making off with over £4 million ($4.63 million) of art, first reported local outlet Il Centro.

	About 30 artworks belonging to Lilli Petroli owner Mauro Lilli were stolen in the unusual heist, including bas-reliefs attributed to Pablo Picasso, a bronze ballerina sculpture by Giacomo Manzù, paintings by Bruno d’Arcevia of the Italian Manner movement, and pieces by sculptor Mario Moretto. None were ensured, and the collection had been displayed throughout the company’s lobby and offices.
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	Police told local news outlets that thieves used one of the company trucks to smash through the site’s security gate and then spent eight hours combing through the building. “They made a mess,” Lilli told Il Messaggero. “They didn’t spare anything,” he added, noting they also damaged furniture and the floors.

	“It’s not your typical theft-to-order,” observed the founder of Art Recovery International, Christopher Marinello, speaking to Ocula. “It appears to me as some sort of revenge, more of an attack on the company or Mauro Lilli himself,” Marinello explained, pointing to the relatively low-tier artworks, given the high risk and organization involved. Since “Mauro Lilli takes great pride in his art collection … it could be a way to send a message,” he said.

	This would contradict reported suspicions that the thieves were hired by a criminal network specializing in international art trafficking, due to “the impressive logistical organization” of the brazen heist, and that the recognizable artworks may be headed to wealthy private collectors, according to Il Centro.

	Local police and the special Carabinieri Cultural Heritage Protection Unit (TPC) are investigating the case.

title: New York Socialite Tracey Amon Asks Court to Compel Advisor Sandy Heller to Turn Over Papers Connected to Late Ex-Husband’s Art Collection
description: New York’s Tracey Amon filed a request on July 25 in the US District Court for the District of Southern New York to subpoena art advisor Sanford “Sa
body:
New York’s Tracey Amon filed a request on July 25 in the US District Court for the District of Southern New York to subpoena art advisor Sanford “Sandy” Heller. She wants him to turn over documents for use in her lawsuits in Switzerland over the disposition of the assets of her late husband, Maurice Alain Amon, who retained Heller as an advisor starting in 2013.  Heller has been described as “possibly the biggest art advisor in the world,” and reputedly works with Roman Abramovich and Steve Cohen.

	The heir to the company SIPCA, which makes inks used in printing currency, Maurice died at 68 in 2019 while on holiday in Saint Tropez. The filing puts his value at some $600 million in assets and business interests at the time of his death, and asserts that Tracey is looking for her rightful share. The request revolves around Heller’s valuation of the collection.
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	The two married in Hong Kong in 2008 “without signing a marriage contract on that occasion or later,” according to an exhibit. He filed abroad for divorce in 2015 without telling her, says the filing, which claims he secretly removed some 20 artworks, collectively valued at $25 million, from their New York home. He allegedly also spirited away artworks from other residences. He claimed in court filings in 2017 that after losing her key, she took a blowtorch to a lockbox in their Paris home, allegedly leaving a toxic dust over artworks by the likes of Jean-Michel Basquiat, Damien Hirst, Richard Prince, Gerhard Richter, Cy Twombly and Andy Warhol.

	While the divorce was in process, he allegedly executed a will naming Albert Amon, his son from a previous marriage, as his only heir, and his assistant, Silvio Venturi, as executor. The New York Post reported that in 2018, she had won about $123,000 a month in spousal support and a lump sum of about $1.3 million in a Monaco court. He allegedly added other legatees and beneficiaries in a codicil executed in Singapore in 2019. She sued Albert and Venturi in Switzerland in 2020; they also brought an action against her.

	The Justice of the Peace in Lausanne ordered the administration of the estate in December 2024. Administrator Olivier Weniger issued an inventory in December 2025, along with a report from accounting firm KPMG with an evaluation of the art holdings as of 2019 of Artmon, the holding company through which Amon held his artworks, which was registered in the British Virgin Islands. 
	

	“It appears that the value of Artmon’s artworks diminished dramatically during 2019,” says the filing, adding, “This diminution appears to be based at least partially on Heller’s valuation.” Heller reported capital losses of €33.4 million and latent capital gains of €7.5 million, for a loss of about €26 million, or $29.6 million. “But,” says the filing (in bold type and italics), “there is no list of the works Heller actually examined, no methodology provided, and no information as to when Heller did its evaluation.”

	Heller did not immediately return a request for comment.

	Tracey Amon is seeking the complete valuation report and all associated work product, including the list of artworks examined, comparables considered, the valuation methodology, and all relevant correspondence. She also seeks documentation of all of Heller’s dealings with Artmon and the Maurice Amon estate, including any art sales, art purchases, consignments, inventories, invoices, and the like.

	The court has yet to respond to Amon’s request.
